hook.line: Every anecdote has a how: how you learned something, how someone walked in, how things slowly changed. Spanish says all of that with the *-ando* and *-iendo* form you already use after *estoy*.
hook.es: Hernando aprendió a manejar manejando el taxi de su papá.
hook.en: Hernando learned to drive by driving his dad's taxi.

examples.en: I learned Spanish by watching films.

rule:
You know *estoy hablando*. The same *-ando* / *-iendo* word can also stand on its own, next to another verb, and then it does three jobs.

How you did it (English by + -ing):
*Aprendí español viendo películas.*
Spanish has no word for by here. The *-ando* form says it alone.

What else was going on (English while + -ing, or just -ing):
*Llegó cantando.* *Vale cocina escuchando música.*

Slowly, bit by bit: *ir* + the *-ando* form.
*El café va mejorando.* It's getting better, gradually.
Compare *va a mejorar*: it's going to get better. The little *a* changes everything.

One thing it never does: be a thing. English says Swimming is good; Spanish uses the plain verb: *Nadar es bueno.* Same after *me gusta*: *Me gusta cocinar.*

A pronoun sticks on the end and the word takes an accent: *riéndose*, *mirándola*.
smallPrint: Teachers call the *-ando* / *-iendo* form the gerund (*el gerundio*). Used alone like this, it is an adverbial gerund; *ir* + gerund is a periphrasis of gradual progress.

readAndPick.es: Superé el miedo hablando con la gente.
options: I got over my fear by talking to people.
I got over my fear to talk to people.

yourTurn.prompt: Choose *viendo* or *ver* and type the whole sentence (I learned Spanish by watching films): Aprendí español ___ películas.
yourTurn.why: By watching is how you learned, and Spanish says how with the *-ando* / *-iendo* form alone.

yourTurn.prompt: Choose *Nadar* or *Nadando* and type the whole sentence (Swimming is good for your health): ___ es bueno para la salud.
yourTurn.answer: Nadar es bueno para la salud.
yourTurn.why: When the action is the thing you're talking about, Spanish uses the plain verb, not the *-ando* form.

yourTurn.prompt: Choose *va mejorando* or *va a mejorar* and type the whole sentence (the café is slowly getting better): El café ___ poco a poco.
yourTurn.answer: El café va mejorando poco a poco.
accept: Poco a poco el café va mejorando.
yourTurn.why: *Ir* + the *-ando* form is change in progress; *va a mejorar* would be a promise about later.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: I learned to cook by watching my mom.
yourTurn.answer: Aprendí a cocinar mirando a mi mamá.
accept: Aprendí a cocinar viendo a mi mamá.
yourTurn.why: No word for by: *mirando* on its own tells how.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: Hernando arrived at the café singing.
yourTurn.why: *Cantando* says what he was doing as he came in.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: Things are gradually changing in the neighbourhood.
yourTurn.answer: Las cosas van cambiando en el barrio.
accept: En el barrio las cosas van cambiando.
yourTurn.why: Gradually changing is *van cambiando*: *ir* plus the *-ando* form.

yourTurn.prompt: Join the two into one sentence with an *-ando* form: *Vale cocina. Escucha música.*
yourTurn.why: The second action becomes *escuchando* and rides along with *cocina*.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it about us: *Aprendí español hablando con la gente.*
yourTurn.answer: Aprendimos español hablando con la gente.
yourTurn.why: Only *aprendí* changes; the *-ando* form never changes for the person.

pitfalls.wrong: Nadando es bueno para la salud.
pitfalls.right: Nadar es bueno para la salud.
pitfalls.why: Almost. English uses -ing as a thing; Spanish uses the plain verb, *nadar*.
Don't translate by: the *-ando* / *-iendo* form already means it.
After *me gusta*, the action is a thing you like, so it's the plain verb.
No *a* before the *-ando* form. *Va a* goes with *mejorar* and means going to.

personal: How did you learn something you're good at? Say it with an *-ando* form: *Aprendí a … mirando / leyendo / haciendo …*
